## Encoding the Paradigm Sequence

Film, task, and filler events become later recall candidates through context updating and item-context learning.
Each event updates context and becomes associated with the resulting state.
During later recall, candidate support depends on how strongly studied items are associated with the context states active during retrieval.

Before the simulated film begins, context is initialized to $c_0$, with no item-associated context units active.
Context changes gradually from $c_0$ as the film unfolds, so the earliest film items are encoded in states most similar to it.
Memory matrices are initialized with pre-experimental associations that reflect baseline structure already present before the simulated paradigm begins.
In $M^{FC}$, each item $i$ can cue its paired context unit with weight $1-\gamma$.
In $M^{CF}$, each item is most strongly supported by its paired context unit, with weight $\delta$.
The other item-associated context units provide weaker background support to that item, with weight $\alpha$.
The start state $c_0$ initially provides no item support in $M^{CF}$.
The initial entries of $M^{FC}$ and $M^{CF}$ are therefore:
$$
M^{FC}_{pre}(j,i) =
\begin{cases}
1 - \gamma & \text{if } j = i + 1 \\
0 & \text{otherwise}
\end{cases}
$$ {#eq-mfc-pre}

$$
M^{CF}_{pre}(i,j) =
\begin{cases}
0 & \text{if } j = 0 \\
\delta & \text{if } j = i + 1 \\
\alpha & \text{if } j > 0 \text{ and } j \neq i + 1
\end{cases}
$$ {#eq-mcf-pre}

When event $i$ is encountered, its representation $f_i$ retrieves context input through feature-to-context memory:

$$
c_i^{\mathrm{IN}} = M^{FC} f_i .
$$ {#eq-context-input}

Context then drifts toward the normalized input.
The coefficient $\rho_i$ keeps context normalized after the update:

$$
c_i = \rho_i c_{i-1} + \beta_{\mathrm{enc}} \widehat{c}_i^{\mathrm{IN}} .
$$ {#eq-context-update}

Each event also encodes associations between its item features and the current context state.
Feature-to-context learning updates $M^{FC}$ so later cues or sampled items can reinstate associated context:

$$
\Delta M^{FC} = \gamma c_i f_i^\top .
$$ {#eq-mfc-learning}

Context-to-feature learning updates $M^{CF}$ so later context can support the item during sampling:

$$
\Delta M^{CF} = \phi_i f_i c_i^\top .
$$ {#eq-mcf-learning}

Here, $\gamma$ controls feature-to-context learning.
The context-to-feature learning rate varies with encoding position:

$$
\phi_i = 1 + \phi_s e^{-\phi_d(i-1)} .
$$ {#eq-primacy-learning}

Here, $i=1$ denotes the first encoded event in the full paradigm sequence.
The first event has learning rate $1+\phi_s$; the increment above 1 then declines across later events at a rate determined by $\phi_d$.

Encoding events also have a source feature vector $s_i$ that distinguishes film items from non-film items.
The source component of context follows the same normalized-drift form as temporal context, with source drift rate $\beta_{emot}$.
All items can form associations with the source context active for that event, scaled by a baseline source-learning term $\eta_s$.
For film encoding events, the source-context portion of the context-to-feature update receives an additional $\phi_{\mathrm{emot}}$ scale to reflect stronger encoding of emotional material in the trauma-film paradigm [@talmi2019retrieved; @cohen2022memory].
Task and filler events carry the neutral/default source feature, so they use the baseline source-learning scale without the added film-source term.
We use the same source-encoding parameters throughout and do not compare distressing with neutral film material.
After encoding, film, task, and filler candidates can all enter later recall through the temporal and source-context associations learned for each item.

## Task Encoding After a Film Reminder

After the film-delay period, the simulated paradigm can present film reminders before the task begins.
The reminder phase reinstates film-associated context before task items are encoded.
Task items encoded from that state can later receive support for recall from context that also supports film material.

The reminder phase begins by updating context toward the start state of the film sequence.
Let $c_b$ denote the context state after the break period.
The reminder-phase start update is:

$$
c_{r,0} = \rho_{r,0} c_b + \beta_{\mathrm{rem,start}} c_0 .
$$ {#eq-reminder-start-update}

The model then applies a sequence of film-item reminder cues.
Each item from the film phase is presented as a reminder cue in the order it was encoded.
Feature-to-context memory retrieves reminder input as in @eq-context-input, and context drifts toward that input using the normalized update in @eq-context-update with the reminder drift rate.
Reminder cues update context but do not become recallable items and do not add new context-to-feature learning.
This isolates the reminder's effect to reinstating film-associated context rather than adding new film-item associations.

Task events are then encoded by the ordinary event-learning rules with the reminder-updated context as the starting state.
Task items carry the neutral/default source feature rather than the film-source feature, so they do not receive the added $\phi_{\mathrm{emot}}$ term.
To vary task association strength, the simulations apply a multiplier $m_{\mathrm{task}}$ to context-to-feature learning for task events:

$$
\Delta M^{CF}_{\mathrm{task}} = m_{\mathrm{task}} \phi_i f_i c_i^\top .
$$ {#eq-task-mcf-learning}

This sensitivity manipulation determines how strongly the context active during task encoding later supports task items during recall.
Task items encoded after the reminder become competitors in later recall because they are associated with context states that are also linked to film material.
The associations formed during film encoding remain unchanged.

## Context-Guided Recall and Test-Phase Cues

Both the involuntary-retrieval condition and deliberate recall require film items to be sampled from a candidate set that also includes task and filler items.
At sampling step $j$, the current context state assigns support to each candidate by probing context-to-feature memory:

$$
a_{i,j} = [M^{CF} c_j]_i .
$$ {#eq-recall-support}

The context vector $c_j$ includes both temporal and source-context components.
Candidates already sampled in the current recall period are excluded from later sampling.

Sampling follows a Luce choice rule over the remaining candidates [@luce1959individual]:

$$
P(i \mid \mathrm{continue}) =
\frac{a_{i,j}^{\tau}}{\sum_{\mathrm{remaining}\ k} a_{k,j}^{\tau}} .
$$ {#eq-luce-choice}

Following likelihood-based CMR implementations, stopping is modeled as a position-dependent hazard independent of current candidate support [@kragel2015neural; @morton2016predictive]:

$$
P_{\mathrm{stop}}(j) = \theta_s e^{j\theta_r}.
$$ {#eq-stopping}

This value is bounded to remain a valid probability.
Because stopping is independent of candidate support, interference is read from the identity of sampled items.
A sampled task or filler item takes the place of a possible film sample.

After a candidate is sampled, feature-to-context memory updates temporal context toward the sampled item's associated context.
Let $c_j^{\mathrm{temp}}$ denote temporal context at sampling step $j$:

$$
c_{j+1}^{\mathrm{temp}} =
\rho_{\mathrm{rec},j}^{\mathrm{temp}} c_j^{\mathrm{temp}} +
\beta_{\mathrm{rec}} \widehat{M^{FC} f_{r_j}} .
$$ {#eq-recall-context-update}

The source-context component follows the same normalized update with its own drift rate, $\beta_{\mathrm{rec,src}}$.
Together, these updates let sampled material shape later search.
A sampled film item can keep later sampling near film-associated context.
A sampled task or filler item can pull later sampling toward non-film material.

Test-phase film cues use the same feature-to-context operation without becoming recall outputs.
When a film cue $q$ is presented, the cued item updates context through $M^{FC} f_q$.
The cue is not counted as a recalled item, does not make the cued film item unavailable for later recall, and adds no new learning.
Recall sampling then resumes from the updated context state.

## Deliberate Recall Control Mechanisms

The same sampling rule governs the involuntary-retrieval condition and deliberate recall, with control settings applied before, during, or after sampling.
The control settings only change post-encoding processes, including the retrieval cue, candidate support, or sampled-item carryover.
Crucially, they do not change the film and task associations learned during encoding.
This lets the simulations distinguish retrieval operations that increase film recall overall from those that reduce competition from task items encoded after a film reminder.

At the start of deliberate recall, the instruction to recall the film shifts current context toward $c_0$.
The strength of this shift is set by $\beta_{\mathrm{start}}$.
This favors early film items over candidates associated with the ongoing context at the end of the delay.
This control mechanism can therefore increase film recall.
However, because it still relies on film-associated context to cue candidates, it does not substantially reduce competition from task items encoded after the reminder.

Externalized free recall asks participants to report every word that comes to mind during recall and identify intrusions or repetitions, revealing nontarget memories that enter search even when they are recognized as errors.
In a retrieved-context model of this procedure [@lohnas2015expanding], monitoring occurs after sampling.
A candidate is accepted as a target response when its retrieved context sufficiently matches the context associated with the target list.
Whether accepted or not, the candidate updates the context guiding the next sample.
The present simulations retain this timing but change the consequence of monitoring.
Sampled task or filler candidates update the next retrieval context less strongly.
Let $\kappa_i = 1$ for film candidates and $\kappa_i = \kappa$ for task and filler candidates.
Monitoring scales the temporal- and source-context updates by the same $\kappa_i$.
The temporal-context update becomes:

$$
c_{j+1}^{\mathrm{temp}} =
\rho_j^{\mathrm{temp}}(\kappa_i \beta_{\mathrm{rec}})
c_j^{\mathrm{temp}} +
\kappa_i \beta_{\mathrm{rec}}
\widehat{M^{FC} f_{r_j}} .
$$ {#eq-monitoring-update}

The corresponding source-context update uses
$\kappa_i\beta_{\mathrm{rec,src}}$.
When $\kappa < 1$, sampled non-film candidates still count as sampled outputs, but both context components are updated less strongly toward their associated states.
This reduces carryover from sampled task or filler candidates without changing the candidate support that made them available.
Like start-of-film reinstatement, this operation does not by itself remove task support from film-associated context.

During deliberate recall, the model can maintain a film-category cue that is absent in the involuntary-retrieval condition.
This cue abstracts the kind of semantic or category support used in retrieved-context models of selective recall, rather than updating temporal or source context during retrieval [@polyn2011semantic; @morton2016predictive].
The cue adds support to candidates marked as film items during sampling:

$$
a^{\mathrm{cat}}_{i,j} = a_{i,j} + \omega_{\mathrm{cat}} g_i .
$$ {#eq-film-category-support}

Here, $g_i = 1$ for film candidates and $g_i = 0$ for task and filler candidates.
The indicator $g_i$ is a retrieval-control cue, distinct from the source feature vector $s_i$ used during encoding.
Task and filler candidates can still compete through $a_{i,j}$, but only film candidates receive the film-category increment.
Therefore, unlike start-of-film reinstatement and retrieval monitoring, a maintained film-category cue can reduce the effect of those task competitors on film recall.

The three evaluated control mechanisms therefore enter the same retrieval cycle at different points: start-of-film context reinstatement before sampling, a maintained film-category cue during sampling, and retrieval monitoring after sampling.

## Item Recognition

CMR has been used mainly to model recall, with relatively few extensions to recognition [@healey2016four; @jin2024theory; @lohnas2015expanding].
Here, recognition is represented only at the level of memory evidence: the model does not specify a decision criterion or generate an old/new response.
A presented probe $q$ retrieves associated context through feature-to-context memory, the same pathway used by reminders, cues, and sampled items.
Recognition evidence is the similarity between the retrieved context and the context active during the test:

$$
e_q = (M^{FC} f_q)^\top c_{\mathrm{test}} .
$$ {#eq-recognition-evidence}

This recognition implementation isolates the access difference between recognition and context-guided recall.
Recall must select a film item among candidates supported by context, whereas recognition evaluates a film item supplied by the test.
The simulation stops at recognition evidence because that evidence is sufficient for the present claim: a presented film item can retrieve associated context without first competing with task items for selection.
The model therefore addresses whether task competitors linked to reinstated film-associated context disrupt item-guided access to film context, not how recognition evidence is converted into decisions or how other interventions might disrupt performance.

# Simulations

The simulations examine a schematic delayed reminder-plus-task trauma-film paradigm, with @james2015computer and @kessler2020visuospatial providing procedural examples rather than fitted targets.
The reminder-before-task sequence places task events after reminder-driven reinstatement of film-associated context, making it possible to examine whether those events become competitors during later retrieval.
The core recall target is the model analogue of selective interference: strong task encoding following a film reminder reduces modeled film intrusions more than deliberate film recall.
The involuntary-retrieval condition is a simplified analogue of film material coming to mind without deliberate intent; it does not reproduce diary or laboratory intrusion procedures.
Simulation 1 shows how a task performed after a film reminder attenuates film recall when task items become strongly linked to reinstated film-associated context.
Simulation 2 examines whether interference is reduced when the test presents a candidate film item for judgment rather than requiring that item to be sampled from context.
Simulation 3 then adds the intentionality manipulation by contrasting the involuntary-retrieval condition with deliberate recall and examining control mechanisms that could protect film recall.
Together, these simulations show how selective interference can arise from competitor encoding after reminder-driven context reinstatement and retrieval conditions that differ in how they access or support film material.

## Methodology

The simulations follow a generalization-style modeling logic [@busemeyer2000model; @lohnas2023event].
Core parameters are anchored in an independent affective free-recall dataset [@dupertuys2026ukraine], and no trauma-film outcomes are fitted.
The simulations require default values for context drift, associative learning, sampling, and stopping before the trauma-film manipulations are applied.
Estimating those values from selective-interference data would require the full modeled paradigm together with trial-by-trial recall sequences that identify which film, task, and non-film candidates entered retrieval.
Published trauma-film studies motivate this qualitative target, but they typically report intrusion counts or final memory scores rather than the sequence-level data needed to estimate retrieval competition.
We therefore use an immediate affective free-recall dataset to set the model's core encoding, retrieval, and stopping parameters.

In that dataset, participants who reported concern about the war in Ukraine studied and recalled lists of war-related and neutral photographs [@dupertuys2026ukraine].
The fitted dataset included 123 participants, four lists per participant, 492 immediate recall sequences, and 3,804 scored recall events.
Parameters were estimated from the ordered recall sequences using the model likelihood, yielding a pooled parameter regime rather than separate fits to the selective-interference simulations.
The resulting parameter values provide a starting regime for context-guided recall of affective and neutral photographs.

The simulations used the event sequence shown in @fig-empirical-target.
Across simulations, we varied whether a film reminder preceded the task, how strongly task material was linked to its encoding context, and how the model searched memory during deliberate recall.
Table 1 lists the parameter values used in these simulations.

:::: {#tbl-simulation-parameters}
| Symbol | Value | Role |
|---|---:|---|
| $\beta_{enc}$ | 0.440 | Drift toward item-cued context during encoding |
| $\beta_{\mathrm{start}}$ | 0.766 | Drift toward the start-of-film context during start-of-film reinstatement |
| $\beta_{rec}$ | 0.678 | Drift toward sampled-item context during recall |
| $\beta_{\mathrm{rec,src}}$ | 1.000 | Source-context drift toward sampled-item source context during recall |
| $\gamma$ | 0.468 | Feature-to-context learning |
| $\delta$ | 0.00022 | Initial support from each item's paired context unit |
| $\alpha$ | 0 | Initial background support from other item-associated context units |
| $\phi_s$ | 0.100 | Scale parameter for the primacy profile $\phi_i$ |
| $\phi_d$ | 1.500 | Decay parameter for the primacy profile $\phi_i$ |
| $\tau$ | 3.562 | Luce-choice exponent for candidate sampling |
| $\beta_{emot}$ | 0.696 | Drift toward the active source feature |
| $\phi_{\mathrm{emot}}$ | 0.130 | Added source-context learning for film items |
| $\eta_s$ | 0.050 | Baseline source-context-to-feature learning for all items |
| $\theta_s$ | 0.0123 | Initial scale of the position-dependent stopping hazard |
| $\theta_r$ | 0.372 | Growth of the stopping hazard across sampled outputs |

Default numerical parameter values.
Values are from a pooled eCMR fit to the immediate free-recall sequences from @dupertuys2026ukraine, with $\alpha$ fixed to zero, except for the source-context and primacy settings described in the text.
::::

In all simulations, the model first encodes the paradigm events and then enters retrieval.
Film, break/buffer, task, and filler items are encoded by the CMR operations defined above.
Each simulated trial contains 16 film items, 16 break/buffer items, 16 task items, and 16 filler items unless otherwise noted.
Break/buffer items implement the delay before the reminder or task, and filler items implement the post-task delay.
Equal phase lengths make redistribution across film, task, and filler periods directly comparable.

In everyday life, partial environmental reminders can bring an event memory to mind involuntarily [@berntsen2021involuntary].
Film stills and blurred film images provide controlled laboratory analogues of such reminders in tasks where participants monitor for or deliberately retrieve film memories [@lau2019intrusive; @lau2021selectively; @mcconnell2026testing].
The recall simulations therefore include weak film cues.
A randomly selected film item serves as a cue before the first sampling attempt and after every fourth attempt while recall continues.
Each cue updates temporal and source context with drift .610, obtained by multiplying $\beta_{\mathrm{rec}}=.678$ by a cue-strength multiplier of .90.
These cues are held constant across conditions so that differences reflect whether a reminder preceded task encoding, the strength of task encoding, and retrieval control rather than differences in the cues supplied at test.
Reminder cues and film cues presented during retrieval update context through feature-to-context associations, but add neither recallable items nor new item-context learning.
In context-to-item recall simulations, all encoded film, break/buffer, task, and filler items can enter the retrieval competition.
Retrieval allows up to 48 sampling steps, and sampled items are removed from the candidate set so the same item is not sampled twice.
The simulated retrieval sequence records sampled candidates by type and encoded position, rather than only final film counts.
This convention makes it possible to examine predictions about how interference redistributes recall across the encoded stream, rather than only reporting final recall counts.

Parameter sweeps rerun the full encode-then-retrieve simulation across planned values of a manipulated parameter.
For each condition and manipulated parameter value, the model first completes the phase sequence, then enters retrieval and samples recallable items using @eq-luce-choice and @eq-stopping.
Each cell contains 5,000 simulated trials unless otherwise noted.
When figures plot recall across the encoded stream, they summarize retrieval after the full phase sequence has been encoded.
Serial-position curves plot the proportion of trials in which each encoding position was retrieved, and phase summaries average those proportions within each phase.
Thus, position and phase labels identify encoding positions, whereas recall probabilities refer to subsequent retrieval.

## Simulation 1: Task Association Strength and Context Similarity

Simulation 1 tests whether a film reminder before task encoding makes task items stronger competitors for film memories in the involuntary-retrieval condition.
Retrieval settings are held fixed, so differences across conditions reflect associations formed before retrieval rather than deliberate control.
The simulation varied whether a film reminder preceded the task and whether the association from context to task material was learned at its baseline strength or twice that strength.
The later recall test used the same weak film cues in every condition.
Without a pre-task reminder, the model received neither the initial shift toward film-onset context nor the subsequent sequence of film-item cues; both reminder drift rates were zero.
With a reminder, the model first shifted temporal and source context toward the states present at the beginning of film encoding (drift = .766).
The 16 film items were then presented once in their original order as reminder cues, each shifting temporal and source context toward the state associated with that item (drift = .440).
These reminder cues changed the context active before task encoding but created no new item-context associations or recallable items.
The association from context to task material was learned at baseline strength ($m_{\mathrm{task}}=1$) or twice that strength ($m_{\mathrm{task}}=2$).
These values test whether the results depend on the strength of task learning; they do not represent particular intervention tasks or levels of engagement.

::: {#fig-simulation1-unguided-sequence fig-pos="H"}
![](work/simulation1_unguided_cued/simulation1_unguided_cued_sequence_summary.png){width=100%}

**Simulation 1: modeled film intrusions by reminder condition and task association strength.**
Reminder condition and task association strength were crossed while all trials used the involuntary-recall condition; weak film cues were supplied periodically during recall in every condition.
**(A)** Example generated recall sequences for each condition.
Each row shows one simulated trial selected near the condition mean for the number of film items recalled; recalled items are ordered left to right by output position.
Colors mark film items, task items, delay/filler items, and unfilled output positions.
**(B)** Mean number of film items recalled across all simulated trials.
The bracket marks the larger reduction from weak to strong task encoding when the task follows a film reminder.
Film recall was lowest when a film reminder preceded strong task encoding, characterizing interference in the involuntary-recall condition.
:::

@fig-simulation1-unguided-sequence shows the aggregate result.
Film recall is lowest when strong task encoding follows a film reminder, and task output increases in the same condition.
The film loss therefore reflects redistribution toward task competitors under fixed retrieval settings.
@fig-simulation1-recall-distributions shows that the redistribution is position-resolved.
Without a pre-task film reminder, increasing the task encoding multiplier produces only modest film loss and task gain, because task items become associated with later context states reached after drift away from the film.
With a pre-task film reminder, the same task-encoding manipulation produces a larger drop in film-position recall and a larger rise in task-position recall.
In other words, the effect of stronger versus weaker task associations is greater with than without the pre-task reminder (i.e., the two factors interact).

::: {#fig-simulation1-recall-distributions fig-pos="H"}
![](work/simulation1_unguided_cued/simulation1_unguided_cued_recall_distributions.png){width=100%}

**Simulation 1: Strengthening task associations after a film reminder shifts recall from film to task items.**
Reminder condition and task association strength were crossed while all trials used the involuntary-recall condition; weak film cues were supplied periodically during recall in all conditions.
**(A)** Without a pre-task film reminder, recall probability by encoded position changes only modestly when task associations are strengthened.
**(B)** With a pre-task film reminder, stronger task associations reduce recall from film positions and increase recall from task positions.
Curves compare weaker and stronger task associations; shaded bands mark film, break, task, and filler positions, and the green vertical line marks the pre-task film reminder.
Task association strength therefore changes recall probability by encoded position most clearly when task encoding follows a film reminder.
:::

Because the reminder reinstates film-associated context before task encoding, increasing task association strength makes that context more likely to support task items during later recall.
Film-item associations remain unchanged; film recall falls because the retrieval context now also supports task competitors.
Simulation 1 therefore shows how task items encoded after a film reminder can become competitors for film memories in the involuntary-recall condition within a retrieved-context model.
Simulation 2 examines the simpler boundary case in which recognition supplies the candidate item instead of requiring context to generate it.

## Simulation 2: Recognition

The recognition simulation uses the same reminder conditions, task association strengths, and resulting item-context associations as the recall simulations.
It changes the retrieval operation by presenting each candidate film item as a test probe rather than requiring that item to be sampled from context.
Context-guided recall requires a film item to be sampled from the candidates supported by current context.
Recognition begins with a presented candidate item and asks whether the context retrieved by that item supports its occurrence in the film.

Each simulated test presented the 16 studied film items and 16 unstudied foil identities in random order.
The foils carried the same broad film-source feature as the studied items but lacked study-specific item-context associations.
Because item features are localist, the foils do not represent graded perceptual or semantic similarity to studied film items.
Each probe retrieved associated temporal and source context through feature-to-context associations, and the match of each component to current test context contributed equally to recognition evidence [@healey2016four; @jin2024theory].
Evidence was calculated before the probe updated test context using the common .90 cue-strength multiplier.
This procedure tests whether linking task items to film-associated context reduces the evidence advantage for studied film probes after the candidate has been supplied.
Decision criteria and confidence remain outside the present implementation.

::: {#fig-recognition-test-format fig-pos="H"}
![](work/simulation4_recognition_full_figure/item_context_recognition.png)

**Recognition supplies the film candidate rather than selecting it among competitors.**
**(A)** CMR stores bidirectional associations between item features and context.
Feature-to-context memory lets an item reinstate its associated context, whereas context-to-feature memory lets context cue candidate items.
**(B)** When film-associated context cues items, film items and task items linked to that context can both receive support.
When a film item reinstates context, retrieval targets context units instead, so task items are not competitors in that step.
**(C)** In recognition, the test presents a candidate film item as the probe.
The probe retrieves associated context, which is compared with ongoing test context; stronger matches provide stronger evidence that the item appeared in the film.
**(D)** Old-film minus foil recognition evidence is plotted across the same reminder conditions and task association strengths used in the recall simulations.
The measure subtracts mean evidence for film-source-matched foils from mean evidence for studied film probes.
Strong task encoding after a film reminder does not produce a corresponding reduction in recognition-evidence separation.
:::

@fig-recognition-test-format shows the resulting test-format consequence.
Strong task encoding after a film reminder strongly reduces context-guided film recall but does not produce a corresponding reduction in recognition-evidence separation.
Old-film minus foil evidence remains essentially unchanged across the four combinations of reminder presence and task association strength, ranging from .640 to .642.
In context-guided recall, film and task candidates can compete whenever the retrieval context supports both.
Recognition reverses that access route: the presented film candidate retrieves associated context directly, so task items do not compete to be retrieved in place of the film item.
The simulation therefore identifies a test-format confound in designs that compare involuntary tests measuring whether film material comes to mind with voluntary tests that supply film material for recognition.
Such designs therefore do not isolate retrieval intentionality: preserved recognition alongside reduced intrusions may reflect a difference between test formats rather than a general sparing of voluntary recall.

Recognition therefore establishes a test-format boundary without resolving the harder recall-control problem: deliberate recall must still generate film candidates while task competitors remain eligible for sampling.
Simulation 3 asks which control operations can protect deliberate recall under that competition.

## Simulation 3: Control Mechanisms for Deliberate Recall

Simulation 3 examines how deliberate retrieval control can protect film recall across the same reminder conditions and task association strengths used in Simulation 1.
It first compares the involuntary-retrieval condition with deliberate film recall across that design, then evaluates which retrieval-control operations account for the relative protection of deliberate recall.
In the involuntary-retrieval condition, start-of-film reinstatement and the maintained film-category cue are absent, and every sampled item updates context at full strength: $\beta_{\mathrm{start}}=0$, $\omega_{\mathrm{cat}}=0$, and $\kappa=1$.
The full deliberate-control condition combines all three operations.
The instruction to recall the film shifts context toward the state present when film encoding began with $\beta_{\mathrm{start}}=.766$.
During sampling, the maintained film-category cue adds $\omega_{\mathrm{cat}}=1$ to the support for every film candidate.
After a task or filler item is sampled, retrieval monitoring uses $\kappa=.5$, so that item carries half of its ordinary temporal- and source-context update; sampled film items continue to update context at full strength.
The main readout is how much strengthening task associations reduces film recall in each reminder condition, rather than total film recall alone.

::: {#fig-simulation2-control-cued-behavioral fig-pos="H"}
![](work/simulation2_control_cued_behavioral/simulation2_control_cued_behavioral.png)

**Simulation 3: deliberate film recall is relatively preserved when a film reminder precedes strong task encoding.**
Reminder condition and task association strength were crossed as in Simulation 1 while retrieval mode was varied between the involuntary-retrieval condition and deliberate film recall.
Deliberate film recall combined start-of-film context reinstatement, a maintained film-category cue, and retrieval monitoring.
Weak film cues were supplied periodically during recall in all conditions.
Rows compare retrieval modes, columns compare reminder conditions, and paired bars compare weak versus strong task encoding.
In the with-reminder column, brackets label the larger reduction in modeled film intrusions and the relative preservation of deliberate film recall.
Strong task encoding reduced film recall most clearly when it followed a film reminder, but this reduction was much larger in the involuntary-retrieval condition than during deliberate film recall.
The model therefore simulates a selective interference effect: strong task encoding after a film reminder substantially reduces modeled film intrusions while leaving deliberate film recall relatively preserved.
:::

@fig-simulation2-control-cued-behavioral demonstrates the model's simulation of the selective interference effect.
In the involuntary-retrieval condition, strong task encoding produces a small film-recall loss without a pre-task reminder and a much larger loss after a film reminder.
Under deliberate film recall, strong task encoding after a film reminder produces a much smaller reduction.
The full deliberate-control setting therefore reproduces the selective-interference pattern under the same learned task competitors.

To decompose the full deliberate-control condition, we evaluated all eight combinations of start-of-film reinstatement, the maintained film-category cue, and retrieval monitoring.
When an operation was absent, its setting was $\beta_{\mathrm{start}}=0$, $\omega_{\mathrm{cat}}=0$, or $\kappa=1$, respectively.
When present, start-of-film reinstatement used $\beta_{\mathrm{start}}=.766$, the maintained cue used $\omega_{\mathrm{cat}}=1$, and monitoring used $\kappa=0$.
Because $\kappa$ specifies how much of a sampled non-film item's ordinary context update is retained, $\kappa=0$ prevents task and filler samples from updating subsequent temporal or source context.
The decomposition therefore evaluates monitoring at its maximal setting, whereas the anchor comparison above uses the moderate setting $\kappa=.5$.

::: {#fig-simulation2-retrieval-control-decomposition fig-pos="H"}
![](work/simulation2_retrieval_control_decomposition/simulation2_retrieval_control_decomposition.png){width=100%}

**Simulation 3: different retrieval controls preserve film recall to different degrees.**
Each control setting was evaluated in two conditions: a low-interference condition with no pre-task reminder and weak task encoding, and a high-interference condition with a pre-task film reminder and strong task encoding.
Weak film cues were supplied periodically during recall in all conditions.
The figure shows all eight combinations of start-of-film reinstatement, a maintained film-category cue, and retrieval monitoring.
The control setting with none of these operations is the involuntary-retrieval condition.
Bars show mean number of film items recalled for each control setting in both conditions.
Start-of-film reinstatement and retrieval monitoring increase film recall in some conditions, but the loss from the low- to high-interference condition is smallest when a maintained film-category cue is included.
:::

@fig-simulation2-retrieval-control-decomposition decomposes how retrieval-control operations alter the film-recall loss produced when a film reminder precedes strong task encoding.
The figure compares film recall in a low-interference condition, with no reminder and weak task encoding, against film recall in a high-interference condition, where a film reminder precedes strong task encoding.
When the maintained film-category cue is absent, film recall remains much lower in the high-interference condition.
Start-of-film reinstatement and retrieval monitoring can raise film recall, but the loss between the low- and high-interference conditions remains large.
When a maintained film-category cue is active, the loss remains below one film item across the tested control settings; with all three controls present, film recall drops by about half an item.
The maintained film-category cue most strongly reduces this loss by helping film candidates overcome competition from task competitors.
In the model, the maintained film-category cue does not alter temporal context or the associations learned during encoding; it adds support to film candidates during sampling, providing a basis for selection that task competitors do not receive.

Because @fig-simulation2-retrieval-control-decomposition compares only the no-reminder/weak-task and reminder/strong-task endpoints, we also evaluated all four combinations of reminder condition and task-association strength.
For each control setting, we asked whether it reduced the additional cost of strong task associations following a reminder, relative to involuntary retrieval.
With the maintained film-category cue removed, none of 121 combinations of start-of-film reinstatement and monitoring, ranging from absent to maximal, reduced this reminder-specific cost.
Restoring the maintained cue reduced the cost, both alone and in combination with reinstatement and monitoring.
Thus, within the fitted model examined here, reinstatement and monitoring could raise film recall but did not account for the relative protection of deliberate recall.

::: {#fig-simulation2-start-context-reinstatement fig-pos="H"}
![](work/simulation2_start_context_reinstatement/simulation2_start_context_reinstatement_film_positions_candidate.png)

**Simulation 3: start-of-film context reinstatement favors early film positions.**
The high-interference condition was held fixed: a pre-task film reminder preceded strong task encoding, the maintained film-category cue was absent, retrieval monitoring was disabled, and weak film cues were supplied periodically during recall.
At recall onset, context either remained in its ongoing state or shifted toward $c_0$ with $\beta_{\mathrm{start}}=.766$ in response to the instruction to recall the film.
**(A)** Probability that the first recalled item came from each encoded film position.
**(B)** Probability of recalling each film position at any point in the search.
Reinstatement produces its largest benefit at early positions, both at recall initiation and across the full search.
:::

@fig-simulation2-start-context-reinstatement shows that the benefit of start-of-film context reinstatement is position-specific: it strongly shifts recall initiation toward early film positions, and its advantage declines across the film sequence.
This positional gradient distinguishes start-state control from a maintained film-category cue, which can support film candidates throughout search.
If the instruction to recall an episode reinstates its initial context, the resulting recall benefit should be greatest for material from early in the episode.

Retrieval monitoring can be distinguished from start-state control and maintained film-category support by examining the order of items recalled.
Because monitoring acts after a non-film item has already been sampled, dampening that item's context update, monitoring limits how much the sample redirects subsequent retrieval.
@fig-simulation2-target-monitoring-diagnostic shows that monitoring increases the probability that a sampled non-film item is followed by recall of a film item.
Monitoring therefore helps recall recover after task or filler material has entered the output sequence.
It does not supply film-directed support before sampling occurs, so it provides only limited protection against task competition during film recall.
Simulation 3 therefore constrains the account: deliberate recall is not spared by a generic voluntary-memory setting.
It is less affected when control supplies film-directed support that task competitors do not share, whereas controls that only change retrieval initiation or post-sampling carryover remain more vulnerable.

::: {#fig-simulation2-target-monitoring-diagnostic fig-pos="H"}
![](work/simulation2_target_monitoring_diagnostic/simulation2_target_monitoring_diagnostic.png)

**Simulation 3: monitoring helps retrieval return to the film.**
These analyses used the high-interference condition: a film reminder preceded the task, and the task material formed strong associations with context.
At recall, the model reinstated start-of-film context but omitted the maintained film-category cue; weak film cues appeared periodically throughout the search.
**(A)** Probability that a film item followed a non-film item as monitoring became stronger.
**(B)** Recall across encoded positions with no monitoring and with the moderate level used in the main comparison above.
Shaded regions show film, break, task, and filler positions; the green line marks the reminder before the task.
Stronger monitoring made retrieval more likely to return to the film after a non-film item.
Because monitoring acts only after that item is sampled, it cannot favor film items beforehand.
:::

# General Discussion

The simulations identify a condition under which goal-directed remembering can remain selective after target-associated context has become linked to competitors.
A film reminder made subsequently encoded task items retrievable from film-associated context, reducing film recall when search relied on that context.
Recognition produced a separate form of preservation because the candidate film item was presented before its associated context was evaluated.
The model distinguishes three ways in which a retrieval instruction could regulate search: by reinstating an episodic starting context before sampling, maintaining information that favors targets during sampling, or limiting the influence of off-target samples on subsequent retrieval.
The operations may act together during deliberate recall, but the simulations separate them to identify their effects.
Start-of-film reinstatement changed where search began, and monitoring helped search return to film material after a non-film sample, but neither made deliberate recall comparably resistant to the learned task competitors.
Relative protection depended on a maintained film-category cue that favored film candidates throughout sampling.
Together, these results locate selective interference in the relation between what has been bound to context and how later retrieval selects or evaluates film material.

## From Contextual Competition to Selective Retrieval

Context binding creates both access and interference.
Reinstating a prior context before new learning can link later material to the earlier episode, allowing the earlier context to cue both sets of events [@hupbach2008dynamics; @sederberg2011human].
Film-associated context can therefore remain available while becoming less diagnostic of film material.
Research on category-directed recall provides a complementary principle: people can maintain semantic or category information that favors target memories while temporal associations continue to organize retrieval [@polyn2011semantic; @norman2017neuronal; @lohnas2026specialized].
Work on selective recollection places a further constraint on this account.
@moccia2022cue found target-selective recollection only when test cues overlapped more with the targeted than the competing source, even though pictures were remembered better regardless of which source was targeted.
A multivariate analysis of the same experiments found that neural reinstatement could favor the competing source when the external cue matched it, whereas later recollection-related activity was more closely aligned with the current goal [@moccia2025effects].
Together, these findings suggest that goal-directed remembering remains selective when retrieval can supplement shared context with information that favors targets over competitors.

This account changes what the selective-interference effect can establish about memory architecture.
Dual-representation accounts attribute the selective pattern to stronger disruption of sensory-bound representations associated with intrusive re-experiencing than of contextualized representations proposed to support coherent deliberate recollection [@brewin2010intrusive; @brewin2014episodic].
The retrieved-context model includes a change in stored associative structure: task events acquire new associations with film-associated context while the learned film associations remain available.
Retrieval goals and test format then determine how strongly those new competitors affect performance.
Preserved deliberate memory therefore does not determine whether the intervention selectively spared one film representation while disrupting another.
Sensory-bound and contextualized representations may still contribute to trauma memory, but the selective-interference contrast alone does not identify their contribution.

The protection produced by the maintained film-category cue depends on an explicit modeling commitment.
The implementation gives every film candidate additional support while task and filler candidates receive none.
At the psychological level, this operation represents a maintained film-category cue of the kind implicated in category-directed recall; the simulations do not derive how participants construct that cue or which film features it contains.
Task association strength has a similarly delimited role.
Following established CMR parameterizations of encoding priority, it scales newly learned context-to-task associations [@sederberg2008context; @polyn2009context; @talmi2019retrieved].
In the present simulations, it is therefore a sensitivity manipulation that varies competitor learning, not a direct representation of engagement, visuospatial processing, or a particular intervention task.
The simulations consequently establish what follows when competitor learning varies and film-directed support discriminates film from task material.

## Interpreting Selective-Interference Evidence

The recognition analysis changes what the strongest positive selective-interference evidence can establish.
Published demonstrations of reduced intrusion reports with preserved voluntary memory are dominated by designs that use recognition as the voluntary-memory test [@holmes2009can; @holmes2010key; @james2015computer; @kessler2020visuospatial; @lau2021selectively; @asselbergs2024effectiveness].
In the model, a recognition probe does not need to defeat task candidates during context-to-item sampling because the candidate film item is already present.
Preserved recognition can therefore accompany impaired context-guided film recall even when both tests depend on the same learned film associations.
Such evidence establishes that presented film items can still recover useful contextual evidence, while leaving unresolved whether film material remains similarly available during deliberate recall.

Recall-based comparisons improve this inference but do not automatically isolate retrieval intentionality.
Vigilance-intrusion tasks require film material to come to mind, yet they can present film cues and ask participants to monitor specifically for film intrusions [@lau2019intrusive; @lau2021selectively].
External film cues can reinstate film-associated context, and film-monitoring instructions may encourage participants to maintain a film-oriented retrieval state.
The present simulations include weak film cues during recall but do not activate a maintained film-category cue in the involuntary-retrieval condition.
They therefore cannot determine whether vigilance-intrusion-task monitoring engages the same selective support used during deliberate recall.
Mixed findings from more closely matched designs should motivate direct manipulations of cueing and retrieval goals rather than being explained retrospectively as consequences of those factors [@mcconnell2026testing].

Related procedures have been extended beyond analogue trauma films to real-life and occupational trauma, including motor vehicle accidents, emergency caesarean section, refugee trauma, and health-care work during COVID-19 [@iyadurai2018preventing; @horsch2017reducing; @kanstrup2021single; @iyadurai2023reducing; @ramineni2023treating; @kanstrup2024guided; @beckenstrom2026digital].
Evidence for selective interference is heterogeneous across trauma-film studies, as indicated by individual null findings, systematic reviews, and replication attempts [@asselbergs2023systematic; @brennen2021investigating; @hemi2023cognitive; @varma2024experimental; @wessel2025evidence].
The clinical reach of these procedures makes their mechanisms consequential, while the mixed evidence limits the conclusions that can be drawn from any single positive dissociation.
Real-world extensions do not themselves establish that retrieved-context competition explains intervention effects outside the laboratory.

## Testing Competitor Learning and Retrieval Selectivity

The distinction between competitor learning and cue discriminability yields a specific hypothesis about intervention task content.
Engagement may strengthen memory for task events, but it does not determine whether a film-directed cue can distinguish those events from film material.
Tetris and active verbal tasks can be similarly enjoyable or demanding, yet their effects on intrusions have differed across studies, and both have reduced intrusions under some delayed conditions [@holmes2010key; @kessler2020visuospatial; @hagenaars2017tetris].
Imagery-competing tasks may generate strongly encoded task imagery that overlaps with brief film-hotspot memories at the level of visual format, making it relevant as a competitor, while remaining sufficiently distinct in source and content for a maintained film-directed cue to preserve deliberate recall.
The current simulations implement competitor strength through task association strength and source discrimination through film-category support; they do not explicitly represent visual-format overlap.
A strongly learned task should therefore permit selective interference when its contents remain distinguishable from film events, but should impair both involuntary retrieval and deliberate recall when its contents also match the film-directed cue.
Existing task comparisons have not manipulated this property directly.

A category-directed externalized-recall experiment could test these predictions in a standard episodic-memory setting.
Participants would first study blocked focal and alternative categories, such as birds and occupations.
A focal episodic reminder or matched nonfocal control would then precede a separate competitor list whose items are never retrieval targets.
The competitors would be relatively distinct from or overlapping with the focal retrieval cue—for example, furniture versus mammals, using normed and counterbalanced category sets.
A postcue would ask participants to recall either the focal or alternative category while reporting and source-classifying every candidate that comes to mind.
The same focal items would therefore be correct targets when their category was requested and off-target list intrusions when the alternative category was requested.

With cue-distinct competitors, focal-context reminding should reduce focal items more when they appear as off-target outputs during alternative-category recall than when they are deliberately targeted.
With cue-overlapping competitors, the focal cue should also support competitor items, reducing that protection during deliberate focal recall.
A matched reminder-only/no-competitor condition would identify any direct effect of reminding, and competitor memory would be tested only after the primary recall test.
Recording identity, input position, output position, latency, and source classification would allow competitor entries and output transitions to distinguish retrieval initiation, sustained category support, and monitoring.
These off-target outputs would be deliberately elicited list intrusions, not spontaneous involuntary memories in daily life.

## Limitations and Scope

The simulations are qualitative mechanism tests rather than fits to selective-interference data.
Core eCMR parameters were estimated from an independent affective free-recall dataset, but the trauma-film sequence and retrieval settings were introduced to examine the consequences of the proposed account.
The simulations therefore demonstrate that retrieved-context competitor learning and discriminating retrieval support can produce the qualitative pattern.
They do not estimate how often participants use these operations or establish that the operations generated any particular empirical result.
A matched dataset containing externalized film and non-film retrieval sequences would provide a stronger basis for parameter anchoring and model comparison.

Several implementation choices further limit the account.
Task association strength scales context-to-feature learning for task items without deriving that learning from task engagement or task content.
The maintained film-category cue is perfectly selective, whereas real retrieval cues may support some competitors and fail to support some film details.
The recognition simulation stops at item-to-context match evidence.
Its film-source-matched foils are sufficient to test whether task items linked to film-associated context reduce the evidence separation between studied and unstudied film-source probes.
They do not represent graded item similarity, and the analysis does not model false familiarity, false recollection, recollection rejection, confidence, or criterion placement in responses to similar lures [@parks2026unified].
The recall simulations include test-phase film cues but do not represent all monitoring demands of diary or vigilance-intrusion procedures.
Finally, the model addresses episodic retrieval processes relevant to intrusive remembering; it is not a model of PTSD, clinical outcome, or treatment efficacy.

The broader contribution is to connect an account of how competitors become bound to target-associated context with an account of how goal-directed retrieval remains selective.
Context can continue to provide access to an event while losing its ability to distinguish that event from later material.
Deliberate recall can remain relatively protected when a retrieval goal selectively favors targets over competitors throughout search, whereas recognition changes how the target enters retrieval by presenting it for evaluation.
Selective interference in the trauma-film paradigm provides a consequential case for specifying these interactions.
Grounding that case in general memory theory also sharpens the evidence needed to identify memory processes that are distinctive to trauma.
